---
title: "About"
---

A map of the trails in [Pacific Spirit Regional Park](https://metrovancouver.org/services/regional-parks/park/pacific-spirit-regional-park)
(Vancouver, BC) and the streets around it, built for a running group. It's the
first step towards generating routes: turning written directions into GPX and
back, making loops or point-to-point runs of a given distance, and one day
covering every trail in the park with as little backtracking as possible.

## Reading the map

- **Park trails** are coloured by bike access, the same split as the official
  park map: <span style="color:#2a78d6">■</span> shared,
  <span style="color:#eb6834">■</span> hiking only,
  <span style="color:#1baf7a">■</span> not tagged either way.
- Grey lines are streets, sidewalks and paths outside the park. We use them
  sparingly, only to link trails without doubling back.
- <span style="color:#eda100">●</span> **WC** marks toilets and
  <span style="color:#e87ba4">●</span> **W** drinking water, useful when
  planning long runs and aid stations. They come from OpenStreetMap: check
  opening hours and seasonal closures before race day.
- Hover a line for its name. Click it for its tags and a link to it on
  OpenStreetMap.
- The buttons at the top left turn layers on and off, including what we
  removed from the network (red) and links we added (dotted black).

On a phone, the [full-screen map](trail_map.html) is easier to use.

## Routes

The [Routes](routes.qmd) page picks a loop (or out-and-back) from the Park
Centre at the distance you choose: the same route of the day for everyone,
or shuffle for another. Each comes with an elevation profile, written
directions, a GPX file, an image for sharing, and palm-size cards to print
for anyone running without a device. The [Ultra](ultra.qmd) page is one
route over every trail in the park.

### How routes are made and picked

**The routes are made ahead of time, not on your phone.** Each time the site
is built, a script (`07_generate_routes.py`) tries about 13,500 loops from
the Park Centre: out to a random trail junction A, across to another, B,
and back. Each leg takes the cheapest way, where a metre of street costs 3×
a metre of trail, and ground already covered costs 8× more, so legs look for
new trail. Those "random" junctions come from a fixed seed, so the same data
always gives the same routes. Out-and-backs go to a trail junction at half
the distance and back.

**Only good routes are kept:** at least 80% trail, at most 10% street, and
(for loops) at most 15% of the distance run twice.

**Then near-copies are removed.** Many good loops differ only in a short
stretch, so we compare routes by the trail segments they use (a segment is
the stretch between two junctions): the segments two routes share, divided
by all the segments either one uses. The best routes go first (most trail,
least doubling back, fewest streets), and each next route is kept only if it
shares at most **75%** with every route already kept. So any two routes
differ in at least a quarter of their trail, about 2 km on an 8 km loop.
Allowing more overlap would give more routes, but more of them would feel
the same.

**Route numbers are positions in that list.** Loops are sorted shortest
first and numbered L01, L02, … (L01 is the shortest loop); out-and-backs are
OB01, OB02, …. When the data or our edits change and the site is rebuilt,
the list can change, so a number isn't a permanent name for a route.

**The 7–10 km routes cover the park.** Random turn points tend to miss
trails close to the start and at the far north end, so after the library is
built the script adds loops aimed at whatever trail no 7–10 km route runs
yet, until no more good loops can be found:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
coverage = FileAttachment("coverage.json").json()
md`Run as a set, the **${coverage.band_routes} routes of ${coverage.band_km[0]}–${coverage.band_km[1]} km**
(${coverage.added_for_coverage} of them added for coverage) run
**${coverage.band_trail_km} of the park's ${coverage.park_trail_km} km of trail**
(${(100 * coverage.band_trail_km / coverage.park_trail_km).toFixed(1)}%).`
```

Just for fun, here's what they miss. Each bit is too short, or too awkward
to reach, for a good loop, but it's only a few metres if you want to say
you've run the lot. "Map" opens the trail map right there.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<table class="table table-sm">
  <thead><tr><th>Trail</th><th>Length</th><th></th><th></th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>${coverage.uncovered.map((u) => html`<tr>
    <td>${u.trail}</td>
    <td>${u.m} m</td>
    <td>${u.dead_end ? "dead end" : ""}</td>
    <td><a href="trail_map.html#18/${u.lat}/${u.lon}" target="_blank">Map</a></td>
  </tr>`)}</tbody>
</table>`
```

The [Ultra](ultra.qmd) page covers everything, these bits included.

**The route of the day is a shuffle seeded by the date.** The page keeps the
routes that match your choices (type and distance), then shuffles them using
today's date in Vancouver (e.g. `2026-09-27`) as the seed for its random
numbers. The same seed always gives the same shuffle, so everyone who picks
the same settings on the same day sees the same order:

- the first route in today's order is the **route of the day**, and it's
  what you get when the page loads or you refresh;
- **Another route** moves to the next one in the order, so you won't see a
  repeat until you've been through every match;
- at midnight the date changes, and so does the order;
- different settings give a different list to shuffle, and so a different
  route.

Nothing is stored or sent anywhere: every phone does the same arithmetic.
"1 of 42 matching routes" means 42 routes fit your settings, and you're on
the first in today's order.

**Sharing a route.** **Share** opens your phone's share sheet with the route's
name, distance, climb, written directions and a link. The link ends in
`?route=` and a short code that fingerprints the route's exact path, so it
opens that same route (not the route of the day) for whoever you send it to.
Where the phone allows, the GPX file goes along too. If the routes have been
rebuilt since and that exact route is gone, the link falls back to the route
of the day.

## Our edits

OpenStreetMap has more than we run and misses a few links we use, so we keep
a small set of [edits](https://github.com/pstrunners/pstrunners.github.io/tree/main/data/manual):

- NW and SW Marine Drive are the park's edge for us: beach and foreshore
  trails below them are left out, as are a few dead-end stubs, parking-lot
  spurs and school grounds.
- Where a trail crosses W 16th Avenue but OSM never joined the two sides
  (Cleveland Trail; Sword Fern to Douglas Fir), we add the missing link.
- Every build checks that trails still connect across Chancellor Blvd,
  University Blvd and W 16th Ave.

## Data

| Data | Source | Licence |
|---|---|---|
| Trails, streets, toilets, water | [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/relation/11683817) | © OpenStreetMap contributors, [ODbL](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/) |
| Elevation | [NRCan High Resolution DEM](https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/0fe65119-e96e-4a57-8bfe-9d9245fba06b) (lidar, 2 m) | Open Government Licence – Canada |
| Park boundary | [Metro Vancouver open data](https://open-data-portal-metrovancouver.hub.arcgis.com/datasets/regional-parks-boundaries) | Open Government Licence – Metro Vancouver |
| Basemap | [OpenFreeMap](https://openfreemap.org/) | © OpenMapTiles, data © OpenStreetMap contributors |

If a public trail is missing or wrong, the best fix is in
[OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/) itself, so every map and app
gets it. The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/pstrunners/pstrunners.github.io).

Please stay on marked trails and follow the park's rules on bikes and dogs.
